peer_results.rationale: AMD's candidates focus on general third-party IP infringement claims against AMD (defensive posture) and AI/export control regulations. They do not address Qualcomm's specific topic of adverse interpretations of licensing commitments, devaluation of SEPs via SDO policies, or limitations on injunctions/remedies in the context of being a licensor.

comparisons.peer_summary: Litigation to assert IP rights against customers or suppliers could harm customer relationships, while third-party IP litigation, including as a result of licensing activities, could negatively impact business financial condition and results of operations if IP protection is inadequate.
comparisons.comparison: Both Qualcomm and Broadcom disclose that their intellectual property licensing activities expose them to third-party litigation and risks regarding the value of their IP rights. Qualcomm specifically highlights risks from third-party proposals to devalue Standard-Essential Patents (SEPs) and limit remedies like injunctions, which could disrupt its licensing business. Similarly, Broadcom notes that third parties pursue IP litigation against it 'including as a result of our IP licensing business,' and that inability to protect IP could limit royalty collection. Unlike Qualcomm, which focuses on structural changes to patent value via SDO policies, Broadcom emphasizes the direct business impact of litigation on customer relationships and royalty collection resulting from its licensing activities.

sentences.text: Further, some third parties have proposed significant changes to existing intellectual property policies for implementation by SDOs and other industry organizations with the goal of significantly devaluing standard-essential patents.

Others have proposed that injunctions should not be an available remedy for infringement of standard-essential patents and have made proposals that could severely limit damage awards and other remedies by courts for patent infringement (e.g., by limiting the base upon which the royalty rate may be applied).
Conversely, third parties have and may in the future pursue IP litigation against us, including as a result of our IP licensing business.

Any inability to adequately protect our IP could limit the value of our technology, result in the loss of opportunities to sell or license our technology to others or limit our collection of royalty payments, any of which could negatively impact our business, financial condition and results of operations.

comparisons.peer_topic: Intellectual Property Protection and Enforcement Risks
comparisons.peer_summary: Intel faces risks in protecting and enforcing its IP rights due to litigation, varying enforceability, and geopolitical factors, including compulsory licensing. Additionally, licensing practices and industry standard participation may allow competitors to use patents or exhaust rights, impairing IP value.
comparisons.comparison: Qualcomm and Intel both identify regulatory and judicial actions that can restrict their ability to enforce patent rights or limit remedies available for infringement. Qualcomm details proposals to limit injunctions and damage awards for SEPs, potentially devaluing its portfolio. Intel faces similar risks where governments or courts may require 'compulsory licensing of IP rights' or render decisions that limit enforceability. Both companies acknowledge that their participation in industry standards organizations subjects them to these constraints, potentially forcing them to license patents on terms that may not reflect their full value.

sentences.text: Others have proposed that injunctions should not be an available remedy for infringement of standard-essential patents and have made proposals that could severely limit damage awards and other remedies by courts for patent infringement (e.g., by limiting the base upon which the royalty rate may be applied).

In addition, in connection with our participation in SDOs, we, like other patent owners, generally have made contractual commitments to such organizations to license those of our patents that would necessarily be infringed by standard-compliant products as set forth in those commitments (referred to as standard-essential patents).

From time to time, governments adopt regulations and governments or courts render decisions requiring compulsory licensing of IP rights, or governments require products to meet standards that favor local companies.
Our participation in industry standards organizations or with other industry initiatives at times requires us to offer to license our patents to companies that adopt industry-standard specifications.
